title: Blowing up a balloon: related rates of change
examples: Why does a balloon grow slower as it gets bigger?
How fast does the radius of a balloon change?

marks.label: Tiny: grows fast
marks.ask: Why does a small balloon grow so fast?

explain.say: You blow air into a balloon at the same steady rate. Have you noticed it swells fast at first, then seems to grow slowly? This curve shows how fast the radius grows. Look at the yellow mark: a tiny balloon grows very fast.

marks.label: Tiny: grows fast
marks.ask: Why does a small balloon grow so fast?

explain.say: Why? Each puff of air must spread over the whole skin. A tiny balloon has little skin, so the same puff pushes it out a lot. Can you picture the puff spreading over a small skin?

marks.label: Tiny: grows fast
marks.ask: Why does a small balloon grow so fast?

explain.say: Now the cyan mark. The balloon is bigger, with more skin, so the same puff only pushes it out a little. Say you push in 100 cubic centimetres each second. At radius 5 centimetres, the radius grows about 0.32 centimetres per second.

marks.label: Tiny: grows fast
marks.ask: Why does a small balloon grow so fast?

explain.say: At the purple mark the radius is 10 centimetres. The skin is four times bigger, so the radius grows four times slower, about 0.08 centimetres per second. Same air, much slower growth. See the curve flatten?

explain.say: Brilliant! This is called related rates: the rate of volume and the rate of radius are tied together by the sphere's formula. Weather balloons that rise 30 kilometres swell slowly for exactly this reason.

faq.q: Why does a small balloon grow so fast?
faq.a: The air you add spreads over the skin. A small balloon has a small surface, so each bit of air pushes the radius out a lot.
asks: Why does a balloon swell quickly at first?

faq.a: Related rates are two rates of change linked by a formula. For a balloon, volume equals four thirds pi r cubed, so how fast the volume grows decides how fast the radius grows.
asks: What is a related rates problem?

faq.q: How do you work out how fast the radius grows?
faq.a: Rate of volume equals the surface area, 4 pi r squared, times the rate of radius. So divide the air rate by 4 pi r squared.
asks: What is the formula for the balloon radius rate?

faq.q: Why is the surface area in the formula?
faq.a: The derivative of four thirds pi r cubed with respect to r is 4 pi r squared, which is exactly the surface area of the sphere. New air forms a thin shell over that surface.
asks: Why does 4 pi r squared appear?

faq.a: Engineers use them for water filling tanks, shadows growing, ladders sliding and radar tracking planes, whenever two changing amounts are linked.
asks: What are real uses of related rates?

facts: For a sphere, dV/dt = 4πr² × dr/dt, since 4πr² is the derivative of (4/3)πr³.
Doubling the radius of a sphere makes its surface area four times bigger.

quiz.say: Air goes into a balloon at a steady rate. As it gets bigger, its radius grows…
quiz.show: Air goes into a balloon at a steady rate. As it gets bigger, its radius grows…
quiz.why: The same air spreads over a bigger surface, so the radius grows more slowly.

wrong.0: The surface grows, so each bit of air pushes the radius out less.
wrong.2: Volume grows steadily, but radius does not, because volume depends on r cubed.

quiz.say: When a sphere's radius doubles, its surface area becomes…
quiz.show: When a sphere's radius doubles, its surface area becomes…
quiz.why: Area depends on r squared, and 2 squared is 4.

wrong.0: Twice as big would be true for a length, not an area.
wrong.1: 8 times is what happens to the volume, which depends on r cubed.
